title: Polar Area: the Slices Are Triangles

steps.body:
Every integral in C5 sliced a region into **rectangles**. A polar region cannot be sliced that way — it is swept out from the origin, so its natural slice is a thin **wedge**.

And a thin wedge is a **triangle**, not a rectangle. Its area is ½ · base · height ≈ **½ r² dθ**.

**A = ∫ ½ r² dθ.** That ½ is the whole difference, and it comes from the triangle.
Slice it into wedges and count.

widget.prompt: The polar curve r = 2cos θ, from θ = 0 to π/2. Inspect a wedge, then raise the count until the sum lands within 0.02 of the exact area, π/2 ≈ 1.5708.
widget.successFeedback: Look at what one slice IS: a triangle, with two straight sides running back to the origin. Its area is ½r²·dθ — and that ½ is the only thing that separates this from every other integral in the course. Slice, measure ONE slice, add them up: the sentence has not changed at all. Only the shape of the slice has. (And the answer, π/2, is exactly the half-disc of radius 1 that r = 2cos θ actually draws.)
widget.lowFeedback: The sum is under π/2. The RIGHT rule undershoots here, because r is SHRINKING across the sweep — each wedge is measured at its narrow end. Raise the count, or switch rule.
widget.highFeedback: The sum is over π/2. The LEFT rule overshoots for the same reason in reverse — each wedge is measured at its fat end. Raise the count and it will settle.

predict.prompt: What changes when the number of area wedges increases?

options.label: Wedges become thinner and the estimate usually improves
The ½r²·dθ wedge rule is no longer needed

predict.reveal: Refinement narrows each wedge's angle while preserving the same ½r²·dθ wedge rule, bringing the sum closer to the limiting area.

cml.actionGoal: Refine cross-sectional slices and connect their accumulated volume estimate to a limiting integral.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: Change the controlling quantity in this sliceSum away from the successful state. Which invariant remains true, and which visible consequence changes?

explanation.prompt: Why does a wedge sum become an area integral?

options.label: Each wedge contributes its triangle area ½r²·dθ, and refinement takes the sum to a limit.
options.feedback: Exactly—this identifies the governing mechanism rather than only the final pattern.

options.label: Only the outer arc length is needed.
options.feedback: That describes an appearance or shortcut, not the invariant that makes the relationship hold.

options.label: The number of wedges itself is the area.
options.feedback: The live model contradicts that claim when its control is changed.

explanationVariants: A thin wedge of angle dθ and radius r is very nearly a triangle with base r·dθ and height r. Its area is ½·(r dθ)·r = ½r² dθ.
The rectangle-slicing of C5 gave height × width. A wedge gives ½ × base × height, and the ½ never goes away.

widget.prompt: Why does the polar area formula carry a ½?

options.label: A thin wedge is a TRIANGLE, and a triangle's area is ½ · base · height.
options.feedback: Right. Base r·dθ, height r, so the area is ½r²dθ. The ½ is not a convention — it is the triangle.

options.label: Because a polar sweep only ever covers half of the full circle's angle.
options.feedback: The ½ appears whatever the sweep. Integrate all the way round and it is still there.

options.label: To cancel the double-counting where neighbouring wedges overlap each other.
options.feedback: Nothing is counted twice. Each wedge covers its own slice of angle, and the ½ comes from the wedge's SHAPE.

options.label: Because r is squared, so a ½ must balance the extra power of r.
options.feedback: The r² is the two lengths of the triangle. The ½ is separate — it is what makes a triangle half of a rectangle.

explanationVariants: A full circle of radius 3 is r = 3, so A = ∫₀^{2π} ½(9) dθ = 9π. The familiar formula πr² also gives 9π.
The visible circle and the polar integral agree because each narrow sector contributes ½r² dθ.

widget.prompt: Drag the radius until the circle's area reads 9π. Compare that geometric area with the polar integral's 9π.
widget.successFeedback: Radius 3 gives area 9π. The polar calculation and the familiar circle formula now land on the same visible region.
widget.lowFeedback: The area is below 9π. Increase the radius until its square is 9.
widget.highFeedback: The area is above 9π. Reduce the radius until the area coefficient is 9.

steps.body:
So the sentence from C5 survives intact:

**Slice the region. Measure ONE slice. Add them up.**

Area between curves measured a **height**. A disc measured **πr²**. A washer measured **π(R² − r²)**. A polar wedge measures **½r²**.

The slicing never changed. The summing never changed. Only ever the measurement — and this time the slice is a triangle.

explanationVariants: A = ∫₀^{2π} ½(1 + cos θ)² dθ = 3π/2 ≈ 4.712. Expanding the square and integrating term by term is the only work.
The cos θ term integrates to zero over a full sweep, and the cos²θ term averages to ½ — which is where the 3/2 comes from.

widget.prompt: The cardioid r = 1 + cos θ, swept from 0 to 2π, encloses an area of 3π/2. Give that as a decimal to three places.

commonErrors.feedback: That is 3π — the ½ has gone missing. The area is ½∫(1 + cos θ)²dθ = 3π/2 ≈ 4.712.
That is π. The cardioid encloses 3π/2, which is half as much again.
That is the multiplier 3/2. Multiply by π: 4.712.

steps.body: A quarter of a circle, the polar way.
hints: The circle r = 3 swept from θ = 0 to π/2 is a quarter-disc.
Check it against geometry: a quarter of π(3²) = 9π is 9π/4.
explanationVariants: A = (9/2)(π/2) = 9π/4 ≈ 7.069 — and a quarter of the circle's 9π is exactly 9π/4. The formula and the geometry agree.
Whenever a polar answer can be checked against ordinary geometry, check it. It is the cheapest way to catch a missing ½.

widget.prompt: Find the area swept by r = 3 from θ = 0 to π/2, to three decimals.

commonErrors.feedback: The ½ has gone missing: that is 9π/2. With the ½ it is 9π/4 ≈ 7.069 — and a quarter of the circle's 9π confirms it.
That is the WHOLE circle, 9π. You swept only a quarter of it.
That is 3π/2, the cardioid's area from the previous question. Here r = 3, giving 9π/4.

widget.fallbackFeedback: ∫₀^{π/2} ½(9)dθ = (9/2)(π/2) = 9π/4 ≈ 7.069 — a quarter of the circle's 9π, as it must be.

takeaways: A polar region is swept from the origin, so its natural slice is a thin WEDGE — a triangle, not a rectangle.
A = ∫½r²dθ, and the ½ is the triangle. Losing it is the classic error, and a circle will catch you every time.
Slice, measure one slice, add them up. The sentence never changed; only the measurement did.
steps.teaser: That is the calculus band: derivatives, integrals, the theorem that joins them, series, and curves that refuse to be functions.

concept.body: Picture one thin wedge, running from the origin out to the curve. It is a triangle. Its two straight sides are both r, and its base is the little arc r·dθ. So its area is ½·r·(r dθ) = ½r²dθ — and you add those up.

explanationVariants: Square the radius, halve it. The dθ rides along.

widget.prompt: A polar wedge has r = 4. What is its ½r² measurement?

commonErrors.feedback: That is r² — you forgot the ½. A wedge is a TRIANGLE, so its area carries a half.
That is r/2. Square first: ½(4²) = 8.
